To synchronize means to make two or more things match up perfectly — in timing, in data, or in action — so that they are always in agreement with each other.

The key word here is match. When things are synchronized, they are not just similar or close — they are in precise alignment. Nothing is ahead. Nothing is behind. Nothing is different from what the other has.
The Two Main Flavors of Meaning

This single word carries two slightly different but closely related meanings depending on how it is used.

Flavor 1: To make things happen at exactly the same time.

This is about timing. If you synchronize two events, you arrange them so they occur at the precise same moment — not one before the other, not slightly off, but simultaneously.

Example: Two people in different cities need to open a door at exactly the same second. They synchronize — they coordinate so their actions happen at the same instant.

Flavor 2: To make two things match each other's current state, so they are identical or consistent.

This is about matching content or status, not just timing. Here, you are not necessarily making things happen at the same time — you are making sure that what one thing has or shows is the same as what another thing has or shows.

Example: You edit a document on your phone. Later, you synchronize your phone with your laptop, which means the laptop now has the updated version too. Both devices now show the same thing. They are in agreement.

Imagine two clocks hanging on two different walls. One shows 3:00. The other shows 3:07. They are out of sync — they disagree. Now you adjust one until both show exactly 3:00. You have just synchronized them.

Now take that same idea and stretch it beyond just clocks — you can synchronize music, movements, files, systems, machines, teams, or schedules. The core act is always the same: you bring two or more things into agreement so that they match perfectly and move forward together.
How It Is Used in Different Situations

In everyday life:
When a group of swimmers performs a routine together — every arm movement, every dip, every turn happening in unison — their movements are synchronized. If one person is even a second early or late, the synchronization is broken.

In technology:
When your phone synchronizes with a cloud service, it means your phone sends its latest data to the cloud, and the cloud sends any updates back to your phone, so both now hold the exact same information. Neither is outdated. Neither is missing anything the other has.

In audio and video:
When you watch a video and the actor's lips move perfectly in time with the words you hear, the audio and video are synchronized. If you've ever watched a video where the voice and lips don't match up, that is a loss of synchronization — commonly called being "out of sync."

In the workplace:
When two teams working on the same project synchronize, they share updates, align their progress, and make sure no one is working with outdated information or going in a different direction.
What It Means to Be "Out of Sync"

Understanding the opposite helps sharpen the meaning. When things are out of sync, they have drifted apart — one has moved ahead, one has fallen behind, or one has changed while the other hasn't. To synchronize is to correct that drift and bring them back into alignment.
Important Nuance: It Is an Active Process

Synchronization does not happen by accident. To synchronize is a deliberate action — someone (or some system) actively makes it happen. Two clocks on opposite sides of the world will drift apart over time. Left alone, they go out of sync. Someone has to step in and synchronize them.

This is why the word carries a sense of effort and intention. You are not just noticing that two things match — you are making them match.

Synchronization can refer to a one-time act or an ongoing process.

A one-time act: "We synchronized our watches before the mission." It happened once, at that moment.

An ongoing process: Your email app constantly synchronizes in the background, pulling in new messages and updating in real time, so what you see always reflects the latest state of things.

To synchronize means to deliberately bring two or more things into perfect alignment — either so they happen at exactly the same time, or so they hold the same information or state — ensuring that nothing is ahead, behind, or out of agreement.
